newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: General's freedom revives old S.African divisions.
newsitem.headline: General's freedom revives old S.African divisions.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela said on Friday the acquittal of retired General Magnus Malan would not slow the pursuit of apartheid's criminals, but former white president F.W. de Klerk said Malan should not have been in the dock in the first place.
"This was a case which never should have happened," said de Klerk, whose term as president partly overlapped Malan's term as defence minister.
"It was clear right from the outset...that the grounds on which the prosecution was based were flimsy and somewhat far- fetched," he said at a news conference.

In the most important trial of South Africa's post-apartheid era, Malan and others accused of masterminding and carrying out the 1987 killing of 13 blacks, including six children, were acquitted on Friday.

The judge said members of the Inkatha Freedom Party, armed and trained secretly by the South African military to fight their common foe the then-banned African National Congress, had doubtless carried out the attack, but not necessarily the six men accused of pulling the trigger.

The state had also claimed the planning for and blessing of the death squad went right up the ladder to Malan, but the judge said there was no evidence the military had plotted the attack on the house of an ANC sympathiser.
Mandela, who ousted de Klerk in elections in 1994, told reporters after the verdict that his government would continue the quest for truth and justice.

"We give the assurance that where persons have died as a result of atrocities, we will continue to investigate who was responsible and who, in regard to alleged 'third force' activities, was responsible for directing these activities."
He urged South Africans to accept the judge's ruling.

Malan's trial, before the acquittal, was portrayed by Mandela's African National Congress as confirmation that political violence between rival black groups in the 1980s and early 1990s was orchestrated by a shadowy "third force" from the white security establishment.
The defence acknowledged during the trial that the white minority government had supported Inkatha, led by Mangosuthu Buthelezi, in its feud with the Communist-aligned ANC.
De Klerk hailed the verdict as a triumph of justice and said the ANC should now act against those of its members who had ordered bombings as part of the black liberation struggle.
"We don't want to see ANC members protected while prosecutions are pursued against the National Party -- We want even-handedness," he said.
Praising Malan as a man of courage who had wanted to prove his innocence in court despite the risk of conviction, de Klerk said: "He took this humiliation like a man."
Justice Minister Dullah Omar told Reuters: "As far as I am concerned there has been a proper judicial process."

He said, however, that human rights offenders should not be tempted by Malan's acquittal to shun Archbishop Desmond Tutu's truth commission, which can give amnesty to those who confess apartheid crimes.

"People who have second thoughts about testifying to the commission should know that if they fail to do so and evidence comes to light that they have been involved in crime, they will be charged," he said.
Omar said there was evidence that a large number of state documents had been shredded during the last days of white rule.
"It is a matter of great concern and I am sure that the destruction of documents does play a role in preventing proper evidence from being placed before the courts."
ANC justice spokesman Johnny de Lange said he feared there could be a backlash against the courts.
"Women and children were murdered brutally on this occasion. The very fact that the criminal justice has failed to bring people to book will have tremendous ramifications," he said.
